courses.title: Course for AP® Calculus AB
courses.summary: A 36-week course organized by the eight units of the current AP® Calculus AB framework: limits, derivatives and their applications, integration and accumulation, differential equations, and applications of integration.
courses.scopeNote: An original Liminal course aligned unit by unit to College Board's course and exam description, with a unit test for each unit and a print-first practice exam in the May 2027 format. Topic numbers identify alignment only; every explanation and problem is original. It is not an authorized AP course, which requires the AP Course Audit, and it does not award credit or predict an AP score.
prerequisites: Complete Trigonometry or precalculus: function families, composition and inverses, radians, and exact trigonometric values.
Simplify rational and radical expressions, solve equations and inequalities, and keep domain restrictions.
Read graphs, tables, and verbal descriptions of functions and interpret average rates of change with units.
outcomes: Reason about limits and continuity from graphs, tables, and formulas.
Differentiate fluently, including composite, implicit, and inverse functions, and interpret derivatives in context.
Analyze functions and solve optimization and related-rates problems with written justification.
Interpret definite integrals as accumulated change, solve separable differential equations, and compute areas and volumes.
Write complete justifications with and without a graphing calculator.
courses.nextStep: Continue with further single-variable calculus, multivariable calculus, statistics, or calculus-based physics. Check the receiving course's actual prerequisites.
courses.referenceNote: The AB exam supplies no formula sheet. The review weeks list what to know.
courses.calculatorNote: Each test part is marked No calculator or Graphing calculator, matching the exam's split.

units.title: Limits and Continuity
units.focus: Describe what a function approaches near an input and connect limits to continuity and asymptotes.
learning: Estimate limits from graphs and tables and determine them algebraically, including with the squeeze theorem.
Classify discontinuities, confirm continuity on an interval, and apply the Intermediate Value Theorem with its conditions.
activities: Compare a table, a graph, and a formula for the same original function near a removable discontinuity.
Write a continuity argument that checks all three conditions at a point.
evidence: Determine a limit and name the procedure that justifies it.
Apply the Intermediate Value Theorem after stating why it applies.
units.bridge: Limits of difference quotients define the derivative in Unit 2.

units.title: Differentiation: Definition and Fundamental Properties
units.focus: Define the derivative as a limit and build the basic differentiation rules.
learning: Interpret average and instantaneous rates, estimate derivatives from tables and graphs, and relate differentiability to continuity.
Apply the power, sum, product, and quotient rules and the derivatives of trigonometric, exponential, and logarithmic functions.
activities: Shrink secant intervals in a table to estimate an instantaneous rate with units.
Find inputs where an original piecewise function is continuous but not differentiable.
evidence: Write the limit definition behind a given derivative value.
Differentiate products and quotients accurately and simplify.
units.bridge: Composite and implicitly defined functions need the chain rule in Unit 3.

units.title: Differentiation: Composite, Implicit, and Inverse Functions
units.focus: Differentiate composite, implicit, and inverse functions.
learning: Apply the chain rule and implicit differentiation.
Find derivatives of inverse and inverse trigonometric functions and higher-order derivatives.
activities: Decompose original composite functions before differentiating.
Find a tangent line to an implicitly defined curve.
evidence: Select and apply a differentiation procedure and explain the choice.
Find the derivative of an inverse function at a point from a table.
units.bridge: Derivatives become rates in context in Unit 4.

units.title: Contextual Applications of Differentiation
units.focus: Interpret derivatives as rates in motion and other contexts.
learning: Interpret derivatives with units in straight-line motion and applied settings.
Solve related-rates problems, use local linearization, and evaluate indeterminate limits with L'Hospital's Rule.
activities: Sketch and label a related-rates diagram before writing any equation.
Approximate a value with a tangent line and decide whether it over- or underestimates.
evidence: Interpret a derivative value in a sentence with units.
Verify the indeterminate form before applying L'Hospital's Rule.
units.bridge: Derivatives also reveal the shape of a graph in Unit 5.

units.title: Analytical Applications of Differentiation
units.focus: Use derivatives to analyze functions and to optimize.
learning: Apply the Mean Value and Extreme Value Theorems and find intervals of increase, concavity, and extrema.
Connect the graphs of f, f′, and f″, and solve optimization problems with justification.
activities: Annotate a graph of f′ to answer questions about f.
Model and solve an original optimization problem and verify the extremum.
evidence: Write a first- or second-derivative-test justification.
Use the candidates test on a closed interval.
units.bridge: Accumulation reverses differentiation in Unit 6.

units.title: Integration and Accumulation of Change
units.focus: Interpret accumulation as the definite integral and connect it to antiderivatives.
learning: Approximate accumulation with Riemann and trapezoidal sums and use definite-integral notation and properties.
Apply the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus and find antiderivatives, including by substitution.
activities: Estimate total change from an original rate table with left, right, and trapezoidal sums.
Analyze an accumulation function defined by a graph.
evidence: Evaluate a definite integral with the Fundamental Theorem.
Choose a technique: a basic rule, substitution, long division, or completing the square.
units.bridge: Antiderivatives solve differential equations in Unit 7.

units.title: Differential Equations
units.focus: Model change with differential equations and solve separable ones.
learning: Verify solutions and sketch and reason with slope fields.
Find general and particular solutions by separation of variables and model exponential growth and decay.
activities: Sketch a slope field on a grid and draw a solution curve through a given point.
Solve an original exponential model and interpret its constant.
evidence: Verify that a function solves a differential equation.
Find a particular solution with the initial condition applied.
units.bridge: Integrals measure average value, net change, area, and volume in Unit 8.

units.title: Applications of Integration
units.focus: Use definite integrals to find average value, net change, area, and volume.
learning: Find average values and use integrals for motion and accumulation in context.
Compute areas between curves and volumes by cross sections, discs, and washers.
activities: Sketch a region and a representative slice before writing an integral.
Use a graphing calculator to evaluate an applied integral to three decimal places.
evidence: Set up and justify an area or volume integral.
Interpret a definite integral in context with units.
units.bridge: The review weeks combine every unit before the practice exam.

units.title: Review, practice exam, and next steps
units.focus: Consolidate the eight units, take the practice exam under timed conditions, and target review from its results.
learning: Practice no-calculator and graphing-calculator multiple choice and write complete free-response justifications.
Score the practice exam with its scoring guidelines, record raw points by section and unit, and plan targeted review.
activities: Take the practice exam in two timed sittings and self-score with the scoring guidelines.
Keep an error log by unit and redo missed items a week later.
evidence: Explain each missed item's error and correct it.
Complete an original modeling investigation after the exam.
units.bridge: After the exam, labeled enrichment previews further calculus; it is not AB content.

schedule.title: Change at an instant; limits from graphs and tables
Intermediate Value Theorem and Unit 1 synthesis
Rates of change and the derivative
Differentiability and the first derivative rules
Product and quotient rules; trigonometric derivatives
Chain rule, implicit differentiation, and inverses
Derivatives in context and straight-line motion
Mean Value Theorem, extrema, and increasing intervals
Connecting f, f′, and f″; optimization
Definite-integral notation and the Fundamental Theorem
Long division, completing the square, and choosing techniques
Separation of variables and exponential models
Average value and motion with integrals
Accumulation in context; area between curves
Area with respect to y and several intersections
Volumes by cross sections and discs
Discs about other lines and washers
Review: limits, derivatives, and no-calculator multiple choice
Review: accumulation, applications, and calculator work
Practice exam, self-scoring, and error analysis
Beyond the exam: a modeling investigation
Beyond the exam: enrichment and next steps

exam.name: AP® Calculus AB Exam
exam.delivery: Hybrid digital: multiple choice in the Bluebook app and free response handwritten in a paper booklet. Liminal practice exams are printed.
exam.calculator: Only where a part says so: Section I Part B and Section II Part A require a graphing calculator.
notes: Each free-response question is worth 9 points.
At least two free-response questions use real-world contexts.

courses.title: Course for AP® Calculus BC
courses.summary: A complete first-calculus course in 36 weeks: AB foundations plus integration techniques, differential equations, parametric and polar calculus, vectors, and infinite series.
courses.scopeNote: Original independent preparation organized around College Board’s ten published unit overviews. No prior Calculus AB course is required. BC objective codes are granular Liminal editorial checklists, not official numbered CED topics. This is not an authorized AP course and does not award credit or predict an AP score. Align week 33 before the local examination date and place enrichment afterward.
prerequisites: Complete Trigonometry or precalculus: function families, composition and inverses, radians, and exact trigonometric values.
Simplify rational and radical expressions, solve equations and inequalities, and keep domain restrictions.
Read graphs, tables, and verbal descriptions of functions and interpret average rates of change with units.
outcomes: Reason about limits and continuity from graphs, tables, and formulas.
Differentiate fluently, including composite, implicit, and inverse functions, and interpret derivatives in context.
Analyze functions and solve optimization and related-rates problems with written justification.
Interpret definite integrals as accumulated change, solve separable differential equations, and compute areas and volumes.
Write complete justifications with and without a graphing calculator.
Analyze parametric and polar curves and vector-valued motion.
Determine convergence and use power series with justified intervals and approximation error bounds.
courses.nextStep: Continue to multivariable calculus, differential equations, linear algebra, or proof-based analysis; check local prerequisites.
courses.referenceNote: The BC exam supplies no formula sheet.
courses.calculatorNote: Each test part is marked No calculator or Graphing calculator, matching the exam's split.

units.title: Limits and Continuity
units.focus: Describe nearby and long-run behavior, and use continuity to justify the existence of function values.
learning: Estimate and evaluate limits using tables, graphs, algebra, and the squeeze theorem.
Distinguish infinite limits from limits at infinity and classify discontinuities.
Verify continuity conditions and apply the Intermediate Value Theorem with its hypotheses.
activities: Compare a deliberately misleading table with a graph and a limiting argument.
Repair a piecewise function at a boundary and justify whether a target value must occur.
evidence: Separate function values from one-sided and two-sided limits.
Write a complete continuity or Intermediate Value Theorem argument.
units.bridge: Use this unit’s methods in differentiation: definition and fundamental properties.

units.title: Differentiation: Definition and Fundamental Properties
units.focus: Build the derivative from difference quotients, then establish fluent basic differentiation.
learning: Interpret the derivative as a tangent slope and an instantaneous rate with units.
Estimate derivatives from data and distinguish differentiability from continuity.
Differentiate elementary functions, products, quotients, and trigonometric functions.
activities: Shrink a secant interval and explain the limiting rate.
Compare symbolic derivatives with slopes inferred from supplied graphs and tables.
evidence: Write both equivalent limit definitions and identify the evaluation point.
Choose and execute the relevant rule while preserving the function’s domain.
units.bridge: Use this unit’s methods in differentiation: composite, implicit, and inverse functions.

units.title: Differentiation: Composite, Implicit, and Inverse Functions
units.focus: Differentiate compositions, implicit relations, inverses, and higher derivatives.
learning: Decompose a composite function and retain every chain-rule factor.
Differentiate an implicit relation and find tangent information.
Use inverse-function derivatives, inverse-trigonometric derivatives, and higher derivatives.
activities: Use a supplied table to evaluate a composite or inverse derivative.
Check an implicit tangent against the original relation and its local graph.
evidence: Justify each rule in a multi-step derivative.
State the nonzero-derivative condition needed for a local inverse derivative.
units.bridge: Use this unit’s methods in contextual applications of differentiation.

units.title: Contextual Applications of Differentiation
units.focus: Translate rates, motion, approximations, and changing geometry into derivative statements.
learning: Interpret position, velocity, acceleration, speed, and contextual derivative units.
Build and differentiate a related-rates constraint before substituting current values.
Construct a local linearization and apply L’Hospital’s Rule only to eligible limits.
activities: Label a changing geometric diagram, including which quantities vary with time.
Compare a tangent-line approximation with concavity and a numerical check.
evidence: Give a rate answer with units and a defensible sign.
Name the indeterminate form before using L’Hospital’s Rule.
units.bridge: Use this unit’s methods in analytical applications of differentiation.

units.title: Analytical Applications of Differentiation
units.focus: Justify extrema and graph behavior using derivative signs and theorem hypotheses.
learning: Apply Mean Value and Extreme Value Theorems under their required conditions.
Connect monotonicity, extrema, concavity, and inflection to derivative evidence.
Model and verify optimization solutions and analyze implicit curves.
activities: Reconstruct function behavior from an original derivative graph.
Compare interior critical points, singular candidates, and endpoints in a constrained model.
evidence: Distinguish a candidate from a justified extremum.
Support a graph or optimization conclusion with intervals and derivative tests.
units.bridge: Use this unit’s methods in integration and accumulation of change.

units.title: Integration and Accumulation of Change
units.focus: Connect accumulation with antiderivatives and extend integration to advanced techniques and improper limits.
learning: Represent signed accumulation by sums and definite integrals, including units and estimation bias.
Use both Fundamental Theorem connections, integral properties, and substitution.
Select algebraic preparation, integration by parts, or partial fractions as appropriate.
Define and evaluate improper integrals using limits, splitting at every singularity.
activities: Analyze an accumulation function from a supplied graph and rate table.
Compare plausible integration methods and verify antiderivatives by differentiation.
Explain why an apparently finite calculator output does not establish improper convergence.
evidence: Show the bounds, differential, and method before a numerical integral value.
Determine improper convergence from the necessary separate limits.
units.bridge: Use this unit’s methods in differential equations.

units.title: Differential Equations
units.focus: Model and approximate differential equations, then solve separable initial-value and growth models.
learning: Verify solutions, interpret slope fields, and construct Euler approximations.
Separate variables with equilibrium and domain restrictions retained.
Solve initial-value problems and compare exponential and logistic behavior.
activities: Compare two Euler step sizes with a slope-field prediction.
Analyze equilibria and limiting population in a fully specified original logistic model.
evidence: Substitute the solution and initial condition back into the model.
Explain why dividing by a factor can lose equilibrium solutions.
units.bridge: Use this unit’s methods in applications of integration.

units.title: Applications of Integration
units.focus: Use integrals to quantify averages, motion, regions, solids, and Cartesian arc length.
learning: Distinguish average value, net change, and total change in context.
Select dx or dy slices and split area integrals at necessary intersections.
Model cross sections, discs, and washers about coordinate or shifted axes.
Set up Cartesian arc length with a justified interval and units.
activities: Sketch a representative slice and label its bounds, radii, or cross-sectional dimensions.
Compare a path’s displacement, distance, and geometric length.
evidence: Explain integrand dimensions and interval choices before evaluation.
Justify all splits introduced by signs, curve crossings, or geometric boundaries.
units.bridge: Use this unit’s methods in parametric equations, polar coordinates, and vector-valued functions.

units.title: Parametric Equations, Polar Coordinates, and Vector-Valued Functions
units.focus: Describe planar curves and motion through parametric, vector, and polar representations.
learning: Analyze orientation, parametric first and second derivatives, and tangents.
Integrate vector components and distinguish speed, distance, and displacement.
Convert and trace polar curves, including negative radius and repeated tracing.
Compute polar tangents and one-curve or two-curve areas with justified intervals.
activities: Trace a curve in increasing parameter order and mark a tangent.
Use symmetry, intersections, and tracing information to construct a polar-area integral.
evidence: Check tangent conditions when a parameter derivative vanishes.
Explain why a chosen interval counts each requested region exactly once.
units.bridge: Use this unit’s methods in infinite sequences and series.

units.title: Infinite Sequences and Series
units.focus: Determine convergence and use infinite series as justified representations and approximations.
learning: Separate sequence limits, terms, partial sums, and infinite series.
Choose and justify geometric, nth-term, integral, p-series, comparison, alternating, and ratio tests.
Distinguish absolute from conditional convergence and bound alternating error.
Build Taylor approximations with derivative coefficients and Lagrange error bounds.
Determine power-series radius and endpoints and perform substitution, differentiation, and integration.
activities: Audit a false convergence argument by checking the test’s hypotheses.
Compare Taylor approximations of different degrees with a proved error bound.
Track how substitution and termwise operations change coefficients and convergence intervals.
evidence: Give a named applicable test and its actual limiting or inequality evidence.
Test each endpoint separately and state a valid interval for series operations.
units.bridge: Use this unit’s methods in review, practice examination, and investigations.

units.title: Review, practice examination, and investigations
units.focus: Synthesize the complete course, use practice evidence to repair understanding, and carry out original investigations.
learning: Solve mixed AB foundations and BC extensions under declared calculator conditions.
Prepare for the separate practice exam, score raw points, and classify errors by reasoning cause.
Reassess repaired ideas with fresh tasks rather than answer recall.
Develop and critique models using motion, accumulation, and approximation with explicit assumptions.
activities: Take the separate original practice exam and record raw points by unit and section.
Compare an initial solution, a repaired argument, and a fresh reassessment.
Write a mathematical report using the supplied original investigation data.
evidence: Support corrections with fresh mathematical evidence.
State a model’s assumptions, approximation error, and limits of its conclusions.
units.bridge: Further study may include multivariable calculus, differential equations, and proof-based analysis.

schedule.title: Limits from graphs, tables, and algebra
Infinite behavior and the Intermediate Value Theorem
Derivative definitions, differentiability, and basic rules
Rates in context, motion, and related-rate models
Related rates, linearization, and indeterminate limits
Mean Value Theorem, extrema, and monotonicity
Concavity and connections among derivative graphs
Accumulation, numerical sums, and definite integrals
Algebraic preparation, parts, and partial fractions
Differential equations, slope fields, and Euler approximation
Separation, initial values, exponential and logistic models
Average value, motion, accumulation, and area
Volumes by cross sections, discs, and washers
Parametric arc length and planar vector motion
Alternation, absolute convergence, ratio, and remainders
Taylor and Maclaurin approximations with error bounds
Power series, endpoints, and series operations
Synthesis of limits, derivatives, and integral calculus
Synthesis of BC extensions and timed written reasoning
Practice examination preparation and error analysis
Capstone, mathematical critique, and further study

exam.name: AP® Calculus BC Exam
exam.delivery: Hybrid digital: multiple-choice responses and free-response prompts in Bluebook, with handwritten free-response answers in a paper booklet. Liminal practice examinations are printed.
exam.calculator: Only where a part says so: Section I Part B and Section II Part A require a graphing calculator.
notes: Each free-response question is worth 9 points.
At least two free-response questions use real-world contexts.
The actual examination reports an AB subscore. Liminal reports practice raw points only and does not estimate that subscore.

courses.title: Course for AP® Physics 1
courses.summary: A 36-week algebra-based mechanics course organized by the eight units of the current AP® Physics 1 framework, from kinematics to fluids, with paper investigations in every unit.
courses.scopeNote: An original Liminal course aligned unit by unit to College Board's course and exam description, with a unit test for each unit, a print-first practice exam in the May 2027 format, and Liminal's own formula reference. Topic numbers identify alignment only; every explanation, investigation, and problem is original. It is not an authorized AP course, which requires the AP Course Audit, and it does not award credit or predict an AP score.
prerequisites: Complete Geometry; take Algebra 2 before or alongside this course.
Solve linear and quadratic equations, rearrange formulas, and use right-triangle trigonometry.
Read and make graphs, and report quantities with SI units and sensible precision.
outcomes: Model motion, forces, energy, momentum, rotation, oscillation, and fluids with diagrams, graphs, and equations.
Choose a system and justify which quantities are conserved.
Design and analyze investigations: linearize data, interpret slopes, and identify sources of uncertainty.
Translate between representations, and between qualitative claims and quantitative reasoning, in written arguments.
courses.nextStep: Continue with further physics, such as electricity and magnetism or calculus-based mechanics, or with chemistry. Check the receiving course's actual prerequisites.
courses.referenceNote: The exam supplies an equation sheet. Use Liminal's reference while learning, and practice with College Board's sheet from the exam page before the exam.
courses.calculatorNote: Four-function, scientific, or graphing calculators are allowed throughout, as on the exam.
courses.labNote: College Board's AP® Physics course framework calls for at least 25% of instructional time in hands-on laboratory work. The paper investigations here use supplied original data; they do not replace that lab work and do not satisfy the AP Course Audit or college lab-credit requirements.

units.title: Kinematics
units.focus: Describe motion in one and two dimensions with vectors, graphs, and equations.
learning: Distinguish scalars and vectors and relate displacement, velocity, and acceleration.
Represent motion with graphs and equations, analyze relative motion, and resolve projectile motion into components.
activities: Turn a position–time graph into a velocity–time graph and a written description.
Paper investigation: linearize supplied position–time data to find an acceleration.
evidence: Choose and apply a kinematic relation with a stated sign convention.
Explain how a reference frame changes a measured velocity.
units.bridge: Forces explain changes in motion in Unit 2.

units.title: Force and Translational Dynamics
units.focus: Explain motion with forces, systems, and Newton's laws.
learning: Choose systems, locate centers of mass, and draw free-body diagrams.
Apply Newton's laws with gravitational, friction, spring, and tension forces, including in circular motion.
activities: Draw free-body diagrams for each object and for the combined system in a two-block problem.
Paper investigation: analyze supplied spring-stretch data to find a spring constant.
evidence: Identify Newton's third-law pairs and justify them.
Solve a multi-object or incline problem from free-body diagrams.
units.bridge: Energy accounts for the same interactions in a different way in Unit 3.

units.title: Work, Energy, and Power
units.focus: Account for energy transfers with work and conservation of energy.
learning: Compute kinetic energy, work, and potential energy for a chosen system.
Apply conservation of energy with energy bar charts and compute power.
activities: Draw energy bar charts for a system before and after a change.
Paper investigation: relate supplied release heights and speeds through a linearized graph.
evidence: Explain how the choice of system decides whether a force does external work.
Solve a multistep problem that includes nonconservative work.
units.bridge: Momentum describes collisions where energy alone is not enough (Unit 4).

units.title: Linear Momentum
units.focus: Use momentum and impulse to analyze interactions and collisions.
learning: Relate impulse to change in momentum, including from force–time graphs.
Apply momentum conservation and classify collisions as elastic or inelastic.
activities: Find impulse as the area under an original force–time graph.
Paper investigation: analyze supplied collision data for momentum and kinetic energy.
evidence: Justify when a system's momentum is conserved.
Classify a collision from kinetic energy before and after.
units.bridge: Rotational versions of motion and force follow in Unit 5.

units.title: Torque and Rotational Dynamics
units.focus: Describe rotation and explain it with torque and rotational inertia.
learning: Relate angular and linear quantities and use rotational kinematics.
Compute torque and rotational inertia and apply rotational equilibrium and Newton's second law in rotational form.
activities: Balance an original meterstick problem with several torques.
Paper investigation: linearize supplied hanging-mass data to find a rotational inertia.
evidence: Choose an axis and justify the sign of each torque.
Solve a pulley problem in which the pulley has mass.
units.bridge: Rotational energy and angular momentum extend the conservation laws in Unit 6.

units.title: Energy and Momentum of Rotating Systems
units.focus: Extend energy and momentum conservation to rotating systems.
learning: Compute rotational kinetic energy and work done by torque, and analyze rolling.
Apply angular impulse and conservation of angular momentum, including for orbiting satellites.
activities: Compare objects rolling down the same incline with energy reasoning.
Explain a spinning skater's change in speed with angular momentum.
evidence: Justify when angular momentum is conserved.
Relate orbital speed and radius for a satellite.
units.bridge: Restoring forces produce oscillations in Unit 7.

units.title: Oscillations
units.focus: Model simple harmonic motion with forces, graphs, and energy.
learning: Identify restoring forces and find the periods of springs and pendulums.
Represent SHM with graphs and equations and analyze its energy.
activities: Match position, velocity, and acceleration graphs for an oscillator.
Paper investigation: linearize supplied pendulum data to estimate g.
evidence: Predict how mass, amplitude, or length changes a period.
Explain energy transfers within an oscillating system.
units.bridge: Fluids apply forces and conservation laws to continuous matter in Unit 8.

units.title: Fluids
units.focus: Apply density, pressure, Newton's laws, and conservation laws to fluids.
learning: Relate density and pressure, including pressure with depth.
Apply buoyancy, continuity, and Bernoulli's equation.
activities: Draw a free-body diagram for a partly submerged object.
Paper investigation: analyze supplied flow data from a draining container.
evidence: Explain buoyant force with pressure differences.
Apply continuity and Bernoulli's equation to an original pipe.
units.bridge: The review weeks connect the eight units before the practice exam.

units.title: Review, practice exam, and synthesis
units.focus: Consolidate the eight units, take the practice exam under timed conditions, and target review from its results.
learning: Practice multiple choice and each free-response type: mathematical routines, translation between representations, experimental design and analysis, and qualitative/quantitative translation.
Score the practice exam with its scoring guidelines, record raw points by section and unit, and plan targeted review.
activities: Take the practice exam in two timed sittings and self-score with the scoring guidelines.
Synthesis investigation with supplied data, plus an optional household-materials version with safety notes.
evidence: Explain each missed item's error and correct it.
Design an investigation and analyze its supplied data in writing.
units.bridge: After the exam, synthesis investigations connect mechanics to further study.

schedule.title: Scalars, vectors, and motion in one dimension
Systems, center of mass, and free-body diagrams
Newton's second law: multi-object systems and inclines
Conservation of energy and energy bar charts
Rotational kinematics and its link to linear motion
Newton's second law in rotational form
Rotational kinetic energy and work by torque
Simple harmonic motion: definition, frequency, and period
Buoyancy and Newton's laws in fluids
Review: experimental design and written reasoning
Practice exam, self-scoring, and error analysis

exam.name: AP® Physics 1 Exam
exam.delivery: Hybrid digital: multiple choice in the Bluebook app and free response handwritten in a paper booklet. Liminal practice exams are printed.
exam.calculator: A four-function, scientific, or graphing calculator is allowed in both sections.
notes: Free response has one question of each type: Mathematical Routines (10 points), Translation Between Representations (12 points), Experimental Design and Analysis (10 points), and Qualitative/Quantitative Translation (8 points).

courses.title: Course for AP® Physics C: Mechanics
courses.summary: A 36-week calculus-based mechanics course organized by the seven units of the current AP® Physics C: Mechanics framework. Calculus may be studied at the same time: week 1 builds a calculus toolkit, and later weeks teach each technique in context when it is needed.
courses.scopeNote: An original Liminal course aligned unit by unit to College Board's course and exam description, with a unit test for each unit, a print-first practice exam in the May 2027 format, and Liminal's own formula reference. Topic numbers identify alignment only; every explanation, investigation, and problem is original. It is not an authorized AP course, which requires the AP Course Audit, and it does not award credit or predict an AP score.
prerequisites: Take Calculus AB or Calculus before or alongside this course.
Complete Trigonometry: vectors, right-triangle trigonometry, and radian measure.
Solve systems of equations and rearrange symbolic relations.
outcomes: Describe motion with derivatives and integrals of position, velocity, and acceleration.
Apply Newton's laws to systems with variable and resistive forces.
Use work–energy, impulse–momentum, and angular momentum relations, computing work, impulse, and rotational inertia by integration where needed.
Analyze simple harmonic motion and pendulums, and design investigations with linearized data.
courses.nextStep: Continue with calculus-based electricity and magnetism, further mathematics such as multivariable calculus or differential equations, or engineering coursework. Check the receiving course's actual prerequisites.
courses.referenceNote: The exam supplies an equation sheet. Use Liminal's reference while learning, and practice with College Board's sheet from the exam page before the exam.
courses.calculatorNote: Four-function, scientific, or graphing calculators are allowed throughout, as on the exam.
courses.labNote: College Board's AP® Physics course framework calls for at least 25% of instructional time in hands-on laboratory work. The paper investigations here use supplied original data; they do not replace that lab work and do not satisfy the AP Course Audit or college lab-credit requirements.

units.title: Kinematics (with a calculus toolkit)
units.focus: Build a calculus toolkit and describe motion with derivatives and integrals.
learning: Interpret rates as derivatives and accumulation as area and antiderivatives, keeping units.
Relate position, velocity, and acceleration by differentiation and integration, and analyze relative motion and motion in two or three dimensions.
activities: Find velocity and acceleration from an original polynomial position function.
Paper investigation: estimate velocities from supplied position data and compare them with a fitted model.
evidence: Recover displacement from a velocity–time graph as an area.
Differentiate a position vector component by component.
units.bridge: Newton's laws, including forces that vary, follow in Unit 2.

units.title: Force and Translational Dynamics
units.focus: Apply Newton's laws to systems, including variable and resistive forces.
learning: Locate centers of mass, including by integration for continuous objects, and draw free-body diagrams.
Apply Newton's second law with forces that depend on time, position, or velocity, and analyze circular motion.
activities: Verify a proposed velocity function for an object slowed by a resistive force.
Paper investigation: analyze supplied terminal-speed data.
evidence: Use a = v dv/dx to relate force and position.
Find a center of mass from a linear density.
units.bridge: Work as an integral of force leads to energy methods in Unit 3.

units.title: Work, Energy, and Power
units.focus: Use work integrals, potential energy functions, and energy conservation.
learning: Compute work as an integral and relate force to potential energy through F = −dU/dx.
Apply conservation of energy and compute power, including from energy diagrams.
activities: Read equilibrium and turning points from a potential energy graph.
Paper investigation: find the work done by a supplied nonlinear spring force.
evidence: Evaluate a work integral for a position-dependent force.
Classify an equilibrium from a potential energy curve.
units.bridge: Impulse as an integral and momentum conservation follow in Unit 4.

units.title: Linear Momentum
units.focus: Analyze interactions with impulse integrals and momentum conservation.
learning: Compute impulse as an integral of force over time.
Apply momentum conservation, center-of-mass motion, and collision analysis in one and two dimensions.
activities: Find impulse from an original force function.
Analyze a two-dimensional collision with components.
evidence: Justify momentum conservation for a chosen system.
Find the velocity of a system's center of mass.
units.bridge: Rotation, with torque as a cross product, follows in Unit 5.

units.title: Torque and Rotational Dynamics
units.focus: Describe rotation and explain it with torque and rotational inertia found by integration.
learning: Relate angular and linear motion and compute torque as a cross product.
Find rotational inertia by integration and with the parallel-axis theorem, and apply rotational equilibrium and dynamics.
activities: Integrate r² dm for an original rod with nonuniform density.
Paper investigation: linearize supplied angular-acceleration data.
evidence: Find a torque's magnitude and direction.
Apply the parallel-axis theorem.
units.bridge: Rotational energy and angular momentum follow in Unit 6.

units.title: Energy and Momentum of Rotating Systems
units.focus: Extend energy and momentum conservation to rotation, rolling, and orbits.
learning: Compute rotational kinetic energy and work by torque, and analyze rolling with and without slipping.
Apply angular impulse, conservation of angular momentum, and energy reasoning to orbits.
activities: Compare rolling and sliding objects on the same incline.
Analyze a collision between a moving object and a pivoted rod.
evidence: Justify when angular momentum is conserved about a chosen point.
Relate orbital energy, speed, and radius.
units.bridge: Oscillations follow in Unit 7.

units.title: Oscillations
units.focus: Model simple harmonic motion with differential equations, energy, and pendulums.
learning: Verify solutions of the SHM differential equation and relate the period to system properties.
Analyze energy in oscillators and the periods of simple and physical pendulums.
activities: Verify a proposed position function for an oscillator by substitution.
Paper investigation: analyze supplied physical-pendulum periods.
evidence: Find the period of a physical pendulum from its rotational inertia.
Explain energy transfers within an oscillating system.
units.bridge: The review weeks combine the units before the practice exam.

units.title: Review, practice exam, and synthesis
units.focus: Consolidate the seven units, take the practice exam under timed conditions, and target review from its results.
learning: Practice multiple choice and each free-response type: mathematical routines, translation between representations, experimental design and analysis, and qualitative/quantitative translation.
Score the practice exam with its scoring guidelines, record raw points by section and unit, and plan targeted review.
activities: Take the practice exam in two timed sittings and self-score with the scoring guidelines.
Synthesis investigation with supplied data and a calculus-based model.
evidence: Explain each missed item's error and correct it.
Design an investigation and analyze its supplied data in writing.
units.bridge: After the exam, synthesis investigations bridge to further calculus-based physics.

Kinetic energy and work as an integral
Momentum and impulse as an integral
Collisions in one and two dimensions
Rotational kinematics and its link to linear motion
Rotational inertia by integration; parallel axes
Newton's second law in rotational form
Rotational kinetic energy and work by torque
Simple harmonic motion: definition, frequency, and period
Review: rotation, oscillation, and experimental design

exam.name: AP® Physics C: Mechanics Exam
exam.delivery: Hybrid digital: multiple choice in the Bluebook app and free response handwritten in a paper booklet. Liminal practice exams are printed.
exam.calculator: A four-function, scientific, or graphing calculator is allowed in both sections.
notes: Free response has one question of each type: Mathematical Routines (10 points), Translation Between Representations (12 points), Experimental Design and Analysis (10 points), and Qualitative/Quantitative Translation (8 points).
